Spirometry has a long history. John Hutchinson described the vital capacity in 1846 using a water spirometer, measuring thousands of subjects including sailors, firemen and prize fighters, and he related vital capacity to standing height. Later work introduced the timed expiratory volume, and Tiffeneau and Gaensler popularized the ratio of the one-second volume to the vital capacity. Reference equations evolved from single-center studies to large multi-ethnic datasets, and the Global Lung Function Initiative produced equations across the age range. Modern devices use pneumotachographs or ultrasonic flow sensors and report quality grades for each session.

The department policy on preoperative pulmonary function testing has changed several times. Previously, all patients over sixty scheduled for upper abdominal surgery were referred, then the policy was narrowed to those with symptoms, then expanded again after a quality review. The anesthesia group has its own checklist that does not entirely match ours, and the surgical schedulers often order the full panel by default because the order set is easier to use that way. There is a committee meeting next month to reconcile the two documents and to decide who should sign off on the final version.
